She closed the diary and nodded. “I think so. I can’t read whatever language it is in, anyway.” She handed me the diary and said, “Is it important?” Paniula’s diary was heavy in my hands with a rough surface that seemed to prick my skin, letting the words seep through my fingers and into my body. I know how that must sound, but that was what it felt like, and the sensation was so strong, I didn’t hear what the woman said, and merely grunted in response. “I would take that as a yes, my love,” the man said, and I looked up. He caught my eye, smiled, and then made a shooing gesture at the door. “It’s all right, Officer. You look like you’re very busy. Joyce and I were just taking a breather before pushing on for the other village. The one that starts with a ‘T’.” “Tasiusaq,” I said, remembering my manners. “Yes, yes.” The man nodded. “The very same. We came on the cruise ship, you know.” “Yes,” I said. “Dreamcaster.” “The very same.” The man smiled and then turned to the woman. “Joyce, didn’t you say you saw the local police arrive onboard shortly before we left on this excursion?” “I did,” Joyce said. She gave me a stern look, and I guessed that I was unlikely to win her over, and if Atii had been there, it would have been up to her to charm the older woman into thinking I wasn’t really as rude as she might think. But, as I reminded myself, the clock was ticking. I opened the diary to check it really was Paniula’s, and then, seeing my name on the first page, I closed it just as quickly and slipped it into one of the larger pockets in my jacket. I checked the time on my smartphone and estimated that – even with the wind and waves against me – I could still get back to the ship in time to take a quick shower and maybe even borrow a shirt from the crew. I pressed my hand to my pocket and clutched the diary through the fabric. And then, taking a breath, I started to run.

I tried breathing through my mouth as I pushed my way through the cloud, turning my head to the right as I was sure I heard something. Maybe even Gaba’s voice, shouting for me to get down. “On the ground!” Not Gaba. He wouldn’t shout at me in English. “On the damn ground, lady!” And he would never call me a lady. And then, when two bulky shadows charged through the cloud and knocked me off my feet, I knew it wasn’t Gaba, and I guessed, from their voices and their actions, the Americans had arrived. It didn’t matter that my nose was stuffed and clogged. I was never going to be able to breathe with the American kneeling on my chest. “Get off her, now!” I heard the words but considering the lack of oxygen getting to my brain, it could have been a hallucination. As it turned out, it was Gaba. There was a scuffle, and I heard more shouting, more cursing, and the promise of wicked things happening to one man and then the other as a brawl broke out in the cloud of dust around the Viking longhouse. I rolled onto my belly and crawled away from the men fighting around me, barely aware that I had lost both my weapons for the second time in as many hours. But as I crawled, choking on gritty air, the helicopters settled in a farmer’s field to the left of the longhouse. The dust settled too, and I picked myself up, spitting grit and phlegm from my mouth, then wiping my lips with the back of my hand. I blinked, rubbed my eyes, and in the early morning light I saw icebergs in the fjord, and, working back to the shore, I saw the Zodiac I had borrowed still parked on the beach, and Rachael, still wearing her yellow jacket, bobbing about inside the boat. More heavily clad men spilled out of the helicopter and charged towards her. I played to my strengths and my light weight, and ran, determined to head them off. “Petra, wait!” Gaba again, but I didn’t look. I kept going, not slowing for a second. I saw Rachael climb over the side of the boat and push it into the water. The motors were still up, and I guessed the growling I had heard must have been Gaba’s boat. Rachael heaved, and the Zodiac slid deeper into the water, and she scrambled aboard as the boat bobbed, caught by the wind, and drifted into the brilliant, deep blue waters of Qinngua. “Constable!” I should have stopped, but something told me that if I did, something bad was going to happen to Rachael, and I picked up the pace, stripping away from the battle-ready men with their big guns, vests, and helmets, and racing onto the beach. “Don’t do it, honey,” Rachael said as I splashed into the water. “You have to stop. They’re going to shoot, Petra. Don’t…” Rachael ducked as the men fired the first warning shots above her head. They would aim at the boat next, with the intent to puncture and sink it. Unless they had already tried, and they are lousy shots. I might have giggled at that thought, or it might have been the effect of the freezing fjord water reaching my midriff. But when I lunged for the boat, I caught a grip on the safety lines looped along the sides. And then, after another volley of warning shots, Rachael reached over the side and grabbed my wrist. I kicked my feet as she hauled me over the side, until we were both sprawled on Zodiac’s deck, faces pressed to the ribbed metal surface as the men on the beach blasted the buoyancy tubes. Air hissed out of the tubes as they punctured, and Rachael laughed. “What’s so funny?” I said, shouting above the noise of the guns. “Nothing,” she said. “Oh, come on.” I reached for Rachael’s hand. “Don’t leave me in suspense.” “Okay,” Rachael said, following another laugh. “It sounds like I’ve got a bad case of gas.” She rolled her eyes and laughed again. And I joined her, just as another bullet burst another compartment of air. “So, Constable,” Rachael said. “What do we do now?” “First,” I said, pausing as the men on the beach were given the order to cease fire. “First, you need to know you didn’t hurt me. Okay?” “Okay.” Rachael nodded. “And second?” I shook my head and said, “I have no idea.” “What?” “No,” I said. “None.” “You mean, you ran through a storm of bullets, and dived into the frickin’ Arctic Ocean to get on a boat with more holes than a Swiss cheese, and you don’t have a plan?” “No,” I said, and sighed. “Jesus, honey, you are nuts.” “Yes,” I said. “I get that a lot.” I lifted my head – just a little – to peek over the rapidly deflating tubes, and glimpsed Gaba on the beach, hands on his hips, with Saarullik and Taateraaq on each side. Gaba stared straight at me, while the two constables had their backs to the water and their weapons casually pointing at a small group of heavily armed Americans on the beach. “Petra?” Gaba shouted my name from the beach. “Yes?” I lifted my head a little further and then stood up slowly. “The boat’s drifting, Constable. We’re coming to pick you up.” “Got it,” I said. Gaba paused for a second before shouting, “Are you okay?” “Yes.” “Both of you?” “We’re fine,” I said. I watched as another man wearing plain clothes, some might call bland, picked his way between the men on the beach to stand next to Gaba. He carried no weapons but had an impressive bullhorn in his right hand. He held it to his lips and pressed the button to project his voice across the fjord. “Rachael Silk? Can you hear me?” “Yes,” Rachael said as she stood up. “Do you have what we agreed on?” “Yes.” Rachael removed her jacket and held it over the side of the boat, soon to be a raft. I turned around and held my breath, suddenly aware of what she was threatening to do. “I’ve got it. Now, are you going to give me what you promised?” “Yes,” the man said. He lowered the bullhorn for a second as if he was collecting his thoughts and then pressed it to his lips again. “But you’re going to have to trust me, Rachael.” “I can’t do that, Barry.” Barry? There was something about that name. “But we had a deal,” Barry said. “Remember?” “I remember lots of deals. But I don’t remember ever getting what I wanted.” Rachael held the jacket out a little farther over the side. “Maybe it’s time to renegotiate?” “I can’t do that, Rachael,” Barry said. “It’s not an option. It’s non-negotiable, I’m afraid.” “Well, shit, Barry,” Rachael said. “Then I guess there’s nothing more to say.” Rachael tossed the jacket over the side of what was left of the boat, and I watched Paniula’s diary fly out of the pocket. The pages from the guestbook scattered in the wind as the diary slapped onto the water’s surface. “No!” I moved forward, shoving Rachael to one side as I leaped over the flat buoyancy tubes and dived into the water. “Petra!” I don’t know if it was Gaba who shouted. It might have been Rachael. But neither did I care as my fingers grasped the corner of the diary, and I clutched it to my chest as the cold cramped my fingers and I stroked, one handed, back to the sinking boat. “You are certifiable, girl,” Rachael said as she reached for me. “Yes,” I said, teeth chattering as she pulled me over the flat tube and onto the metal deck. “What the hell is so important about that book, anyway?” she said. “I don’t know.” I shivered for a few seconds, trying to speak. And then, as I saw Gaba in a Zodiac racing towards me, I looked at Rachael and said, “I haven’t read it yet.” 
 15 It took six duvets, four hours, and one electric blanket before I felt warm again. Gaba sat in the armchair at the end of the bed, removing grit from my MP5 with a cleaning kit he said he liberated from the Americans. He looked up from time to time, and every time I stirred, he looked at me. I caught his eye, but with my hands curled around the corner of the duvet, I kept my mouth and nose covered, hiding my smile as he watched over me. I would never tell Atii, but not doing something naughty with Gaba, was almost more exciting that doing what I sometimes fantasized about doing with the big, bald, macho leader of Greenland’s SRU. I know. Hopeless. But then, wasn’t it okay to be a hopeless romantic once in a while? “I know you’re awake, Petra,” Gaba said. “My eyes are open.” “Aap. But you’ve been awake for about two hours. Am I right?” I said nothing, preferring not to reveal that I had secretly watched him for almost as long as he had been watching me. He turned his head and nodded at the windowsill, and the bundle of towels within which I hoped I would find Paniula’s diary. “It’s ruined, of course,” he said, and I sighed. “The ink has run on most of the pages, but the deeper you get into the book…” “Yes?” I said, not daring to hope too much. “Well, it’s possible…” “Yes?” “I said it’s possible, Petra, that you might be able to read some of it. When it’s dried out, of course.” “Yes,” I said. “But before then, you’ll want to know about Rachael and the rest of her merry band of diamond smugglers.” “Her band?” “Aap,” Gaba said. “That’s what Barry says.” Gaba raised a thick finger to stop me from talking as he continued. “The three guys were what Barry called pastries, I think.” I giggled, and then pulled the covers down to say, “Patsies. Fall guys. Or dupes.” “Well, whatever they are, he said Rachael picked them up, and paid them a tonne of cash to pretend they were Sean Arnet and Co. She even paid them to stick the diamond jewellery in passengers’ pockets.” I was still processing the thought that there were three patsies, when I realised Gaba had moved on. “…confiscated as evidence, of course,” he said. “What was?” “The jewellery,” Gaba said. “Barry took it all as evidence, and he’s taking it all back to the States, along with Rachael and the three guys.” “It wasn’t fake, then?” “The jewellery?” Gaba shrugged. “Who knows, and who cares? We’re done with this one, Constable.” Gaba slid the MP5 and the cleaning kit onto the table and stood up. “Funny thing about Barry…” “Yes?” “He was a last-minute replacement. Apparently, the other guy who was supposed to lead the operation was sick with something. Barry just happened to be in Greenland, and stepped up, as they say.” “What was Barry’s last name?” Gaba shook his head and said, “I can’t remember. He probably told me. But the thing about him was there was nothing memorable about him. He had brown hair – a little thin, maybe. He wore boring clothes. Nothing stood out. Not even his accent. Everything about Barry was…” “Bland,” I said, cutting Gaba off. “Aap. That’s what I was going to say. “His name is Barry August,” I said, remembering what Rachael had told me in the longhouse. “He’s…” I sat up, suddenly warm and awake, only to grab the duvets again as I discovered I was naked. “Right,” Gaba said. “About that. You were cold, Petra. You were shivering. I had to get your wet clothes off you, and…” I gave Gaba a hard stare and then said, “And what about Saarullik and Taateraaq?” Gaba shook his head. “On the way back to Nuuk. We’re on the next flight, but you can take the ship a little further up the coast if you…” “Yes?” I said. Gaba held up his finger again, and I waited for him to catch on to what I said earlier. It was like watching the dawn break in the far north – a pale light growing stronger and sharper by the second. “What did you say the guy’s name was?” “Barry August.” “August as in…” “Sean Augustus Arnet,” I said, suddenly convinced that it was all starting to make sense. “The man who flew in as a replacement at the last minute and confiscated all the fake diamonds.” “Aap… And…” “Diamonds we think are fake.” “Sure, but all those men with guns, Petra. They were the real deal.” “The real deal who probably just made a hefty bonus on the side on an operation in a country most people have never thought about, or even heard of.” “So you think…” “Yes,” I said. I stood up slowly, covering my body with the bottom duvet, and wrapping it around me as Gaba’s brain was occupied with thoughts of how he had been duped, and might even be one of Sean Augustus Arnet’s pastries. Yes, I enjoyed that one. “But the commissioner…” Gaba said. “He talked to him.” “He talked to someone,” I said. “And we need to know who.” Gaba pulled out his phone and stepped out of the cabin, leaving me alone to peel back the towels and discover just how unreadable Paniula’s diary had become. Several of the pages were stuck together, and I didn’t dare peel them apart for fear of tearing them. But one of the pages was hanging out, and I tugged it free, only to realise it wasn’t a page from the diary, but something else that had been tucked inside. I turned around as Gaba burst back into the room, wearing a look I just knew could only mean trouble. “It’s him,” he said, clenching his fist around his phone. “It was August.” “Barry?” “Aap,” Gaba said. “He called the commissioner. He was the commissioner’s contact. We’ve been set up from the start. It was August’s idea to use Rachael. Can you believe that? He basically told me the play, and how to play it. He must have smuggled the diamonds onto the cruise ship, and then stepped off somewhere. He’s so bland he could have been anyone. But we’re not done…” “Gaba…” “This isn’t over, Petra. The commissioner is just as mad as I am. We’re going to get him. I have no idea how. But it’s a done deal. We’ll get him.” “Gaba, listen,” I said, as I plucked the extra page out of the diary. I waved it in front of him. “And what’s supposed to be?” “It’s what Rachael was going to use to negotiate a better deal with Sean. Or Barry.” I frowned and said, “I’m not sure. But whatever she wanted, he obviously wasn’t going to give it to her. And now…” “Now what?” Gaba said. “Now we’ve got he wants. You want to get him?” Gaba nodded. “Then this is how we do it.” “Right,” Gaba said. He reached for the MP5 and started putting it back together. “Gaba,” I said. “What?” “You’ve got a plane to catch.” He stopped what he was doing and then shook his head. “You mean we. Right?” “No,” I said with a nod at Paniula’s diary. “I have to catch up on my reading.” Gaba took a moment to take the hint, but I shooed him out of the cabin with the promise of delivering the page torn from the guestbook as soon as it was dry. But until then, I was going to try my very best to enjoy a Greenland cruise in the way it was supposed to be done. Slowly. Under the midnight sun. The End
